papers.title: Understanding Double Descent through Universal Compression
papers.label: arXiv:2611.33759v1

summary.background:
- Double descent: test error first rises near the point where a model can just fit its training data, then falls again as the model gets even larger.
- Bias-variance tradeoff: the classical view that test error is U-shaped in model size.
- Maximum likelihood (MLE): fitting parameters that make the observed data most probable.
- Bayesian posterior and ensemble: averaging predictions over many plausible parameter settings rather than using one fitted setting.
- SGD / SGLD: stochastic gradient descent, and a noisy variant that samples from an approximate posterior.
- Cross-entropy loss: a score for predicted probabilities; a uniform guess over 10 classes scores log 10.
- Universal compression: coding data with a single scheme that performs well without knowing the source; regret measures the extra cost versus the best scheme.
summary.one_liner: The paper reinterprets neural-network double descent (test loss rising near the interpolation threshold, then falling again as models grow) through universal compression, bounding the maximum-likelihood excess test loss by four terms and linking the MLE-vs-Bayes gap to an MLE-vs-ensemble gap.
summary.plain: Large neural networks sometimes get worse on new data as they grow, then get better again, which the classical "bias-variance" picture does not predict. This paper explains that pattern using ideas from data compression: it splits the extra test error of a standard fitted model into four pieces. In experiments with random labels, the gap between a standard training method (SGD) and a Bayesian-style averaged predictor (SGLD ensemble) accounts for much of the error peak.
summary.why: Double descent is widely observed but still not well explained for modern deep networks, so a new framework for it is of interest. The text reports the main evidence as experiments with random labels, and the theoretical links depend on assumptions (such as exact posterior sampling and a well-specified setting), so the strength of the conclusion beyond these settings is not established here.

papers.abstract: Many deep learning models exhibit a double-descent phenomenon, where test loss exhibits a sharp peak near the interpolation threshold and then descends a second time as model size grows further, contrary to the U-shape predicted by the classical bias--variance tradeoff. The double-descent phenomenon has been found and explained in toy classical models, but is not well-understood in modern deep learning despite extensive empirical study. We interpret double descent through the novel lens of universal compression. Specifically, we upper bound the maximum-likelihood excess test loss as a sum of four terms: an approximation-and-shift term, a minimax batch regret, a prior cost, and an MLE-vs-Bayes gap. Under exact posterior sampling, we further show that the expected MLE-vs-ensemble gap lower-bounds the MLE-vs-Bayes gap in the well-specified setting. In our experiments, a Gaussian-prior SGLD approximation to the Bayes predictor, unlike SGD, shows no pronounced interpolation peak. Experiments with uniform random labels support this gap as a major contributor to the double-descent peak; here, the SGD cross-entropy is roughly four times the SGLD ensemble cross-entropy at the peak, while the ensemble cross-entropy remains near $\log 10$.

papers.title: Improved Sample Complexity of Robust Reinforcement Learning with KL Uncertainty Sets
papers.label: arXiv:2611.33592v1

summary.background:
- Reinforcement learning: an agent learns a policy (a rule for choosing actions) by trial and reward.
- Generative model: an assumed simulator that can be queried for outcomes from any state-action pair.
- Distributionally robust RL: the agent optimizes for the worst environment within a set of plausible alternatives around its nominal model.
- KL divergence: a measure of how different two probability distributions are; here it sets how far the alternative environments may stray.
- Sample complexity: the number of data samples needed to reach a target accuracy epsilon.
- Discount factor gamma: how strongly future rewards count relative to immediate ones; (1-gamma)^-1 reflects the effective planning horizon.
- Upper and lower bounds: guarantees that enough samples suffice, and that fewer samples cannot work in general.
summary.one_liner: This paper tightens the upper and lower bounds on the number of generative-model samples needed to find an epsilon-optimal policy for distributionally robust reinforcement learning with KL-divergence uncertainty sets, and extends the lower bound to all uncertainty levels.
summary.plain: The paper looks at how much practice data a learning agent needs to make good decisions when the real environment might differ somewhat from its best guess, with the allowed difference measured by a statistical distance called KL divergence. Earlier work left a gap between how much data was known to be enough and how much was known to be necessary, and its lower-bound results only covered a limited range of how far the environment could drift. The authors report a tighter upper bound, a lower bound that holds for any drift level, and say that the two roughly match in several regimes.
summary.why: The work refines theoretical limits on how efficiently robust AI decision-making can be learned, which matters for making such methods reliable when deployed conditions shift. The text is limited to the abstract, so it does not show practical impact or experiments, and the significance beyond theory is unclear from this text alone.

papers.abstract: In this paper, we study distributionally robust reinforcement learning with Kullback--Leibler (KL) divergence-defined uncertainty sets. The goal is to find a policy that maximizes the robust value function, defined as the worst-case value over all transition kernels in the uncertainty set. Assuming access to a generative model, we aim to understand the sample complexity of finding an $\epsilon$-optimal robust policy. The best-known sample complexity results in the literature show a non-trivial gap of $\mathcal{O}\{\max\{p_\wedge^{-1}(1-\gamma)^{-1},(1-\gamma)^{-2}\}\}$ between the upper and lower bounds, where $p_\wedge$ denotes the minimum positive transition probability of the nominal transition kernel, and $\gamma$ is the discount factor. More importantly, existing results on the lower bound only cover a limited range of the uncertainty level. In this paper, we develop tighter and complete upper and lower bounds for robust RL with KL-defined uncertainty sets. Our upper bound is the tightest among all existing studies, and it improves upon the best-known bound by at least the order of $\mathcal{O}(\min\{p_\wedge^{-1},(1-\gamma)^{-1}\})$ for uncertainty level $\delta\in(0,1)$. Furthermore, our lower bound holds for any uncertainty level. Our upper and lower bounds (nearly) match in various regimes, providing improved results for this problem.

papers.title: Instance-Dependent Bandit Convex Optimization in One Dimension
papers.label: arXiv:2611.31608v1

summary.background:
- Multi-armed bandit: choosing where to sample next and learning from noisy rewards.
- Fixed-confidence setting: the learner must stop with a guaranteed error level, and the goal is to minimize the number of samples used.
- Convex function: a bowl-shaped curve with a single lowest point, the minimizer.
- Sublevel set: the set of points where the curve lies below a given height.
- Instance-dependent vs. minimax: instance-dependent bounds depend on the specific problem; minimax bounds are worst-case over all problems in a class.
- Simple regret: how far the chosen point is from the best value.
- Sample complexity: the number of measurements needed.
summary.one_liner: The paper studies instance-dependent sample complexity for one-dimensional stochastic bandit convex optimization in the fixed-confidence setting, showing a matching-rate result for minimizer localization but no comparable instance-dependent gain for simple regret.
summary.plain: The paper looks at how many noisy measurements are needed to find the lowest point of an unknown curve when each measurement is a costly test at a chosen spot. It asks whether the answer depends on how the specific curve is shaped, not just on worst-case bounds. The authors find that locating the minimizer can be done faster on easier curves, while merely finding a point that is nearly as good as the best one cannot be sped up in the same way.
summary.why: The result separates two goals that are often treated as one, which may matter for designing adaptive experiments and sequential testing. The text does not show broader impact beyond this one-dimensional theory, so its reach beyond that setting is unclear.

papers.abstract: We study the instance-dependent sample complexity of one-dimensional stochastic bandit convex optimization in the fixed-confidence setting. First, we consider minimizer localization, where the learner seeks to identify a point within distance $\varepsilon$ of the unique minimizer. We introduce a new instance-dependent quantity $\Delta_\varepsilon(f)$, corresponding to the threshold for which the sublevel set of $f-\min f$ has length $2\varepsilon$. We prove a lower bound of order $\Delta_\varepsilon(f)^{-2}$ and give a bisection-style algorithm that matches this rate up to logarithmic factors. We then revisit the simple-regret setting, where the goal is to identify an $\varepsilon$-optimal point. Surprisingly, no comparable instance-dependent improvement is possible: every correct algorithm has sample complexity of order $\varepsilon^{-2}$ on every instance, matching the minimax rate up to constants. Together, these results separate the statistical complexity of minimizer localization from that of simple-regret optimization in one-dimensional convex bandits.

papers.title: PAC-style Bounds on the Conditional Validity of Conformal Predictors
papers.label: arXiv:2611.33023v1

summary.background:
- Prediction sets: instead of one predicted value, a model returns a range or set of plausible outcomes.
- Coverage: the fraction of cases where the true outcome falls inside the set; the target here is 1 minus alpha (for example 90%).
- Marginal vs. conditional validity: marginal means the rate holds averaged over all inputs; conditional means it holds for each kind of input.
- Calibration data: a held-out sample used to set the size of the prediction sets.
- PAC-style bound: a guarantee of the form "with high probability, the true quantity is at least this large."
- Markov and Cantelli inequalities: standard probability tools that bound how far a random quantity can stray from its average, using only its mean (and variance for Cantelli).
- Hoeffding argument: a classic tool giving finite-sample confidence limits on an average.
summary.one_liner: The paper derives PAC-style probabilistic lower bounds on input-conditional coverage of conformal predictors, using Markov and Cantelli inequalities, and proposes conditional-coverage variance as an estimable measure of conditional validity.
summary.plain: Conformal prediction is a way to output a set of likely answers, rather than a single answer, with a promised long-run success rate. That promise holds on average across all inputs, but it can be off for particular kinds of inputs. This paper gives probability-based guarantees on how well the coverage holds for a given input, using only a finite amount of calibration data.
summary.why: Guarantees that hold for specific subgroups or individual inputs matter in settings such as medical or safety decisions, where average success can hide failures. The text suggests the variance of conditional coverage could serve as a practical check of this, but the abstract alone does not show how well this works in practice.

papers.abstract: Conformal prediction sets are guaranteed to be marginally valid over the attribute space, but local coverage can diverge from the user-defined target $1-\alpha$. Constructing conditionally valid prediction sets with finite calibration data is impossible for a general data-generating distribution. We derive PAC-type probabilistic lower bounds on the input-conditional coverage of any conformal predictor, without assumptions on the data distribution. They are based on the Markov and Cantelli inequalities and adapt to both calibration-marginal and calibration-conditional setups. A tighter, model-dependent Cantelli bound depends on the variance of the conditional coverage and is estimable from data using a fully non-asymptotic Hoeffding argument. The results suggest conditional-coverage variance as a scalable and theoretically motivated empirical measure of conditional validity.

papers.title: Nearly Minimax-Optimal Sample Complexity of Natural Policy Gradient with a Matching Information-Theoretic Lower Bound
papers.label: arXiv:2611.28628v1

summary.background:
- Markov decision process (MDP): a model of sequential decisions where outcomes depend on the current state and chosen action.
- Policy: a rule for choosing actions in each state.
- Horizon H: the number of time steps in an episode; transition kernel: the probabilities of moving between states.
- Generative model: an oracle that lets the learner query any state-action pair for a sampled next state.
- Natural policy gradient: a policy update that takes gradient steps adjusted for the geometry of the policy space.
- Sample complexity: how many samples are needed to reach error ε; minimax/lower bound: a worst-case limit no method can beat.
- Last-iterate guarantee: a performance bound on the final policy, not an average over iterations.
summary.one_liner: This paper gives last-iterate sample-complexity guarantees for sample-based natural policy gradient in tabular finite-horizon MDPs with a generative model, showing an O~(SAH^4/ε^2) upper bound that matches a stated information-theoretic lower bound up to logarithmic factors, plus an iteration lower bound for exact NPG with step size 1/H.
summary.plain: The paper asks how many sampled experiences a learning agent needs to find a nearly optimal decision policy, and whether a particular method that adjusts the policy directly (natural policy gradient) can reach that minimum. The authors build sample-based versions of this method that update the policy by sweeping backward through the time steps, without estimating the transition probabilities. They report that the number of samples needed matches a lower bound on what any method must use in the worst case, up to logarithmic factors.
summary.why: It addresses whether a widely used policy-optimization method can be statistically optimal, which bears on the theory of reinforcement learning. The claim of matching a lower bound is the central point, but the text alone does not let me verify the proofs or compare against the wider literature, so readers should check the technical details.

papers.abstract: A fundamental question in reinforcement learning is how many sampled transitions are needed to learn a near-optimal policy, and whether direct policy optimization can attain this statistical limit. To answer this question, we consider natural policy gradient (NPG), a widely used policy optimization method. We study tabular finite-horizon Markov decision processes (MDPs) with known rewards and unknown horizon-dependent transition kernels, accessed through a generative model. Our sample-based NPG algorithms update the policy by backward sweeps and do not estimate transition probabilities. Under three different batch-size and step size schedules, we establish last-iterate guarantees with sample complexity $\widetilde O(SAH^4/\varepsilon^2)$, where $S$, $A$, and $H$ denote the number of states, the number of actions, and the horizon length, respectively. In this setting, horizon-dependent transition kernels contribute a factor of $H$ to our transition-query bound. Our information-theoretic lower bound of $\Omega(SAH^4/\varepsilon^2)$ shows that the resulting $H^4$ dependence is unavoidable in the worst case, even for agents that select their queries adaptively. To the best of our knowledge, these are the first last-iterate guarantees for NPG whose sample complexity matches an information-theoretic lower bound up to logarithmic factors. Consequently, our results demonstrate that direct policy-space optimization through NPG can achieve the fundamental statistical limits of reinforcement learning while guaranteeing the performance of the final policy. Furthermore, for known kernels, we prove that exact NPG with a constant step size $\eta=1/H$ requires $\Omega(H^2/\varepsilon)$ iterations in the worst case, matching the known upper bound for that step size.

papers.title: Optimal User-Level Private Stochastic Convex Optimization and Mean Estimation with Heavy Tails
papers.label: arXiv:2611.28460v1

summary.background:
- Differential privacy: a guarantee that an algorithm's output barely changes if one person's data is swapped out; (ε, δ) is the standard parameterization, with δ a small failure allowance.
- User-level privacy: protects all samples belonging to one user, not just a single record, which is stronger than item-level privacy.
- Stochastic convex optimization: minimizing a convex loss function using noisy gradient samples drawn from an unknown distribution; "excess population risk" measures how far the result is from the best possible model.
- Lipschitz constant: a bound on how fast a function can change; here it is allowed to be random and unbounded.
- Heavy tails: distributions where extreme values occur more often than in a bell curve, so higher moments may be infinite or hard to bound.
- Moments: summary measures of how large values get (second moment relates to variance, k-th moment to higher tail behavior).
- Mean estimation: estimating the average of a distribution from samples.
- Minimax optimal: the best worst-case rate any algorithm could achieve.
summary.one_liner: This paper gives minimax-optimal excess risk bounds for user-level (ε, δ)-differentially private stochastic convex optimization and mean estimation when per-sample Lipschitz parameters are heavy-tailed, requiring only bounded second and k-th moments, and it closes an approximate-DP gap in directional-moment mean estimation.
summary.plain: The paper studies how to learn a good model from data held by many different users while protecting each user's whole set of records from being revealed. It allows the gradients used in learning to be extremely variable, with occasional very large values, instead of assuming they are capped. The authors report matching upper and lower bounds (up to logarithmic factors) on how accurate the learned result can be, and an algorithm that reaches this with about 1/ε users.
summary.why: Real data often has heavy tails, where a few extreme values break standard privacy guarantees that assume bounded inputs, so relaxing that assumption while keeping optimal accuracy is a meaningful theoretical step. The text presents the results as tight and optimal, and the mean-estimation byproducts improve on prior work by named authors; I cannot judge from the abstract alone how practical the algorithm is.

papers.abstract: We study stochastic convex optimization with heavy-tailed stochastic gradients under $(\varepsilon, \delta)$-user-level differential privacy, which protects each user's entire collection of samples. Instead of assuming a uniformly bounded Lipschitz constant, we only assume bounds on the second- and $k$-th moments of the random sample Lipschitz parameters. This allows for unbounded, heavy-tailed stochastic gradient distributions and can lead to sharper excess risk bounds. We characterize the minimax optimal excess population risk up to logarithmic factors. Our algorithm achieves the optimal rate with only $\widetilde{O}(1/\varepsilon)$ users. As a byproduct of our algorithmic developments, we obtain tight bounds for user-level private mean estimation under norm-moment assumptions, improving over the guarantees of Esfandiari et al. (2022) and Zhao et al. (2024). Finally, for mean estimation under the directional-moment assumption of Agarwal et al. (2025), we close their remaining approximate-DP gap by removing the additional $d/\varepsilon$ user requirement and attaining the optimal sample complexity up to logarithmic factors.

papers.title: Renormalized Entropy from Symmetries: Simplicity Bias and Neural Heat Death
papers.label: arXiv:2611.27889v1

summary.background:
- Parameter symmetry: a change to a network's weights that leaves the computed function identical (for example, rescaling connected layers in a ReLU network).
- Langevin dynamics: a noisy gradient-descent process whose long-run behavior settles into an equilibrium distribution over parameters.
- Gaussian regularization: a penalty that pulls weights toward zero, here with a strength that is taken to zero.
- Low-temperature limit: the regime where the noise is small, so the process concentrates near minima of the loss.
- Entropy (in this context): a measure of how much parameter space corresponds to a given function; more volume means more probability.
- Neural tangent kernel: a linearized approximation describing how a function changes as parameters change; the paper uses it to interpret the "simplicity bias".
- Homogeneous activation: an activation such as ReLU where scaling the input scales the output by the same factor.
summary.one_liner: The paper derives the equilibrium distribution over functions learned by neural networks under Langevin dynamics with weak Gaussian regularization, showing how parameter symmetries induce a renormalized entropy that favors singular, low-rank functions in linear networks and inactive neurons in homogeneous-activation networks.
summary.plain: Neural networks can be reparameterized in many ways that leave the function they compute unchanged, and this paper asks whether those redundancies quietly steer which functions training tends to settle on. The authors study a noisy training process in the limit of vanishing regularization and find that, at nonzero noise, a renormalized "entropy" favors certain functions. In their examples, this pushes linear networks toward low-rank functions and pushes networks with homogeneous activations toward switched-off neurons, which can drive the output toward zero.
summary.why: It offers an explicit account of how symmetry alone can bias what a network learns, a question relevant to understanding generalization and implicit regularization. The text does not show how far these results extend beyond the linear and homogeneous-activation cases it treats, so broader impact is uncertain.

papers.abstract: Neural networks have parameter symmetries: parameter transformations that do not affect the represented function. How do these symmetries affect the functions that neural networks ultimately learn? We study the implicit bias arising from these symmetries by calculating the equilibrium distribution over represented functions under Langevin dynamics with Gaussian regularization. To isolate the effect of symmetries on this distribution, we study the limit in which the strength of the regularization is taken to zero. In certain cases, we show that the zero-regularization and infinite-time limits commute. In the low temperature limit, we recover known effective regularizations. At positive temperature, a renormalization procedure allows us to derive a novel entropy which predicts symmetry-induced preference for certain functions. For linear networks, we obtain explicit entropy terms that favor singular and low-rank functions. For networks with homogeneous activations, we find entropy terms that favor inactive neurons, which can lead to neural "heat death" in which equilibrium mass concentrates on networks with vanishing output. We interpret these results through the neural tangent kernel, as a simplicity bias selecting for functions that vary slowly under variations in the parameters.

papers.title: Verifying and Strengthening Neural Tangent Kernel Theory
papers.label: arXiv:2611.27487v1

summary.background:
- Neural network: a function built from layers of weighted sums and simple nonlinear functions, whose weights are tuned by training.
- Gradient descent / gradient flow: repeatedly nudging weights downhill on an error measure; gradient flow is the continuous-time version.
- Neural tangent kernel (NTK): a fixed similarity measure between inputs that describes how a very wide network changes during training.
- Lazy training: a regime where weights move only slightly from their starting values, so the network acts almost like a fixed linear model.
- Concentration inequalities: bounds stating that random quantities stay close to their average with high probability; the matrix-Bernstein bound is one such tool.
- Operator norm and Hessian: a measure of the largest stretching a matrix or curvature matrix applies; the Hessian describes local curvature of the loss.
- Lean 4: a proof assistant in which mathematical statements and proofs are checked by computer.
- Width: the number of units in a hidden layer.
summary.one_liner: A Lean 4 machine-checked formalisation of the two-layer neural tangent kernel (NTK) convergence theorem for tanh networks, which also tightens the standard concentration-width bounds and flags a Hessian-norm obstacle to the usual linearisation argument.
summary.plain: Very wide neural networks trained by gradient descent are often claimed to behave in a simple, predictable way, and a known theory (neural tangent kernel theory) explains why. This paper rebuilds the main argument for a small two-layer network inside a computer proof assistant, so every step is checked by machine rather than by reading. The authors report that the checked proof holds with explicit width conditions and that the error shrinks exponentially over training time.
summary.why: Checking a standard theory line by line can catch hidden gaps, and the paper reports that its alternative variance bound gives concentration-width certificates 36 to 121 times smaller than the conventional one in the stated settings. The required widths remain far beyond practical sizes, and the text itself says this limits applicability, so the work is best read as a verification and sharpening exercise rather than a practical advance.

papers.abstract: Writing Neural tangent kernel (NTK) theory explains why very wide neural networks trained by gradient methods converge in the lazy-training regime. Its standard proof combines matrix concentration, random Gram matrices, continuous-time dynamics, spectral perturbation, and a bootstrap argument, but has lacked machine-checked verification. We present a Lean\~4 formalisation for two-layer networks, proving an end-to-end theorem: for a smooth bounded activation (instantiated with $\sigma=\tanh$), frozen biases, paired $\pm 1$ initialisation, and explicit width conditions, gradient flow exists uniquely with probability at least $1-\delta$, and $$ \|r(t)\|^2 \leq \|y\|^2 e^{-\lambda_0 t/2}. $$ The sole data assumption is population NTK non-degeneracy, $\lambda_0>0$. Initial coercivity, kernel drift, the movement bootstrap, the residual ODE, and flow existence and uniqueness are formally proved. The formalisation also sharpens the standard analysis in two ways. First, replacing the conventional matrix-Bernstein variance proxy with the classical row-covariance proxy yields estimated concentration-width certificates for $\tanh$ that are $36$--$53\times$ smaller at $(m,d)=(16,8)$ and $94$--$121\times$ smaller at $(32,16)$. Lean certifies the inequality; the ratios are numerical. Second, the network Hessian has operator norm $\Theta(\sqrt{p})$ on the sup-norm parameter ball (a paper calculation), preventing the expected $O(1/\sqrt{p})$ linearisation bound via sup-norm Taylor estimates. An $L^2$ parameter geometry resolves this issue. Required widths remain polynomial but far beyond practical scales, limiting applicability.

papers.title: Class-Conditional Conformal Triage for ICAO Face-Image Compliance under Class Imbalance
papers.label: arXiv:2611.25342v1

summary.background:
- Conformal prediction: a method that wraps any classifier and produces sets or flags with a guaranteed long-run coverage rate (e.g., about 90% of true labels contained).
- Coverage: the share of cases where the true answer is inside the predicted set; "under-covered" means the guarantee fails for some groups.
- Marginal vs. class-conditional (Mondrian) conformal: marginal applies one guarantee across all data; Mondrian applies it separately within each class, which helps rare classes.
- Class imbalance: violations are rare compared with compliant photos, so overall averages can hide poor performance on the rare class.
- False positive: a compliant photo wrongly flagged as a violation.
- Abstention/retake: declining to decide and asking for a new photo.
- Bonferroni correction: a strict adjustment for testing many criteria at once, which makes each criterion's threshold harsher.
- Subject-disjoint split: training and test data use different people, avoiding leakage.
- ICAO/ISO: international standards for passport photo requirements.
summary.one_liner: The paper evaluates class-conditional (Mondrian) conformal prediction as an uncertainty-aware accept/reject/retake layer on top of an ICAO face-image compliance analyser across 14 criteria in the synthetic TONO benchmark, using subject-disjoint splits and logistic classifiers.
summary.plain: Passport-style photos are checked against many rules (such as head position, lighting, and background), and an automatic checker says pass or fail for each rule without saying how sure it is. This paper adds a statistical layer that attaches a measure of confidence to those decisions, so that uncertain photos can be sent for a retake. The authors found that a version that treats each rule's failing cases separately kept coverage close to the target for rare failures, but it did not beat simple tuned abstention rules on false alarms, and checking all 14 rules together with a strict correction forced nearly every photo to be retaken.
summary.why: It addresses a practical gap: rule-based compliance checkers give hard verdicts with no uncertainty, and rare violation classes are where ordinary methods fail. The text reports trade-offs rather than a clear win, so its value is mainly as a worked case study of conformal prediction under class imbalance; wider relevance beyond this benchmark is not shown in the text.

papers.abstract: Automated ICAO/ISO face-image compliance analysers provide criterion-level pass/fail decisions, yet these verdicts do not quantify uncertainty when deciding whether to accept, reject, or retake a photograph. We investigate conformal prediction as a triage layer for BioGaze, evaluating 14 compliance criteria on the synthetic TONO benchmark. Without retraining the analyser, we fit per-criterion logistic classifiers and compare marginal and label-conditional (Mondrian) conformal prediction with conventional abstention rules using subject-disjoint splits. Marginal conformal prediction achieved approximately 0.90 overall coverage but substantially under-covered violations, with a ten-partition mean of 0.37 for one criterion. The corresponding Mondrian means ranged from 0.89 to 0.92 across criteria. However, most of the reduction in criterion-level false positives came from the logistic layer (0.145 to 0.048), while tuned abstention rules achieved lower false-positive rates than Mondrian at comparable retake rates. Bonferroni correction for joint coverage across 14 criteria required retaking nearly all images. These findings show that class-conditional conformal prediction can achieve near-target empirical coverage for minority violation classes and reveal trade-offs between statistical coverage, classification performance, and retake requirements in multi-criterion face-image compliance assessment.

papers.title: Deviations from the NTK Regime in CNNs under Joint Depth-Width Scaling
papers.label: arXiv:2611.25624v1

summary.background:
- Neural network: a function built from layers of weighted sums and nonlinearities, trained by adjusting its weights.
- Convolutional neural network (CNN): a network whose layers apply small sliding filters, common in image tasks.
- Width and depth: width here is the number of channels per layer (C); depth is the number of layers (L).
- Neural tangent kernel (NTK): a matrix describing how changing the weights affects outputs; in the infinite-width limit it stays fixed during training and is deterministic.
- Dispersion: how much the kernel's values vary across random initializations; small dispersion means the kernel concentrates near a single value.
- Initialization regimes: ordered, critical, and chaotic describe whether signals shrink, stay balanced, or blow up as they pass through layers at the start.
- Kernel rotation: how much the kernel's direction changes during training.
- Scaling collapse: when curves measured at different sizes fall onto one curve when plotted against a combined variable such as L/C.
summary.one_liner: Numerical study of how joint depth-width scaling (ratio L/C of convolutional layers to channels) affects neural tangent kernel dispersion at initialization and kernel rotation during training in CNNs.
summary.plain: This paper looks at how a neural network's behavior drifts away from a simplified "infinitely wide" idealization as the network gets deeper relative to its width. The authors ran numerical experiments on convolutional networks and tracked how spread out the network's kernel is at the start and how much it rotates during training. They report that the spread grows with the ratio of depth to channel count in the critical and chaotic initialization regimes, stays small in the ordered regime, and that the kernel rotates more as the ratio grows.
summary.why: It offers a single ratio, L/C, as a candidate quantity governing when the simplified infinite-width picture stops being accurate for CNNs, which matters for anyone relying on that picture to understand training. The text does not show how far the finding generalizes beyond the experiments run, so its wider significance is unclear.

papers.abstract: The concentration and training-time constancy of the neural tangent kernel (NTK) depend on the interplay between network width, depth, and initialization. While joint depth-width scaling has been studied in fully-connected, residual, and recurrent networks, its effects in convolutional neural networks (CNNs) remain less understood. We investigate these effects numerically in CNNs, examining NTK dispersion at initialization and kernel rotation during training. Let depth $L$ be the number of convolutional layers, and width $C$ the number of channels per layer. We find that NTK dispersion increases with $L/C$ in the critical and chaotic initialization regimes, but remains small in the ordered regime. At critical initialization, dispersion curves approximately collapse as a function of $L/C$, suggesting a nontrivial joint scaling regime. During training, kernel rotation generally increases with $L/C$, even in the ordered regime where initial dispersion is small. Together, these results suggest that $L/C$ may govern NTK deviations from the infinite-width limit in certain regimes, and that NTK concentration at initialization and stability during training exhibit different scaling behaviors.

papers.title: Diffusion Models are Provably Efficient Priors for Sparse Recovery
papers.label: arXiv:2611.24602v1

summary.background:
- Sparse signal: a vector where most entries are zero; compressed sensing recovers it from far fewer measurements than its length.
- Linear measurements: each observation is a weighted sum of the unknown signal's entries.
- Ill-posed inverse problem: many different signals could explain the same measurements, so a prior is needed to choose a plausible one.
- Prior: a probability distribution over signals encoding what they typically look like; here a Bernoulli-Gaussian model (each entry is zero with some probability, otherwise Gaussian).
- Diffusion model: a generative model that learns to turn noise into data by reversing a gradual noising process.
- Langevin sampling: an iterative method that moves toward high-probability regions with added random noise, used to draw samples from a distribution.
- Sample complexity: how many measurements are needed for recovery; "near-optimal" means close to the theoretical minimum.
- Total variation distance: a measure of how different two probability distributions are.
- Posterior sampling: drawing signals consistent with both the measurements and the prior.
summary.one_liner: The paper proves that a pretrained diffusion model used as a prior, combined with a likelihood-guided annealed Langevin sampler, can provably recover sparse signals from few linear measurements in polynomial time with near-optimal sample complexity, and gives total variation guarantees for posterior sampling when the signal follows the assumed prior.
summary.plain: The paper studies how to reconstruct a signal that is mostly zeros from a small number of indirect measurements, a classic problem in compressed sensing. It asks whether a generative model trained to produce such signals (a diffusion model) can be used as a guide for this reconstruction, with a theoretical guarantee rather than only empirical success. The authors show that, under stated assumptions, the method recovers the signal efficiently and with a near-minimal number of measurements.
summary.why: Diffusion models are widely used as priors for imaging and sensing problems, but their theoretical behavior has been poorly understood, and prior guarantees were often asymptotic or computationally costly. This work offers finite, polynomial-time guarantees for a clean model problem, which may help explain when such solvers can be trusted; the extent to which the results carry over to real images is not established by the text.

papers.abstract: Diffusion models have transformed generative modeling through their ability to capture and generate samples from complex data distributions. This success has spurred substantial interest in using pretrained diffusion models as expressive priors for highly ill-posed inverse problems in imaging and sensing. Despite strong empirical performance, theoretical understanding of this approach remains limited: existing guarantees are often asymptotic or entail prohibitive computational costs in the worst case. In this paper, we address this gap by studying sparse recovery from a small number of linear measurements, a classical problem in compressed sensing. We show that, given an accurate diffusion model capturing a sparsity-promoting Bernoulli-Gaussian prior, a likelihood-guided annealed Langevin sampler provably recovers the sparse signal in polynomial time with near-optimal sample complexity for a broad family of random and deterministic sensing matrices. When the signal is indeed drawn from the postulated prior, we further establish total variation guarantees for posterior sampling after a final denoising step. These results lay a theoretical foundation for statistically and computationally efficient inverse solvers with diffusion priors.

papers.title: Distribution-Free Uncertainty Quantification for Weather Forecasting: Conformal Prediction Under Spatiotemporal Dependence
papers.label: arXiv:2611.24329v1

summary.background:
- Forecast interval: a range around a predicted value meant to contain the outcome a chosen share of the time (e.g. 90%).
- Conformal prediction: a family of methods that builds such ranges from past errors, with guaranteed average coverage under exchangeability assumptions.
- Marginal coverage: the long-run fraction of cases covered at one location, averaged over time.
- Spatial and temporal dependence: nearby places and consecutive days tend to have correlated errors, which breaks the independence assumptions behind many standard statistics.
- Overdispersion: variance larger than what independent cases would produce; here, the day-to-day spread in the fraction of the map covered.
- ERA5 and HRES: a reanalysis dataset used as the "truth" and ECMWF's operational forecast model; a CNN is a small neural-network forecaster.
- Interval score: a single number rewarding narrow intervals that still cover the outcome, penalising misses.
summary.one_liner: A benchmark of eight conformal prediction interval methods for gridded 2 m temperature forecasts (CNN and ECMWF HRES, ERA5 target), showing that near-nominal marginal coverage hides strong day-to-day and temporal clustering of misses, which is largely driven by days with large errors across much of the grid.
summary.plain: Weather forecasts often come with a "plus or minus" range meant to contain the true temperature a set share of the time. This paper checks whether those ranges are right not just on average over many places, but also within a single day across the whole map and across consecutive days. The authors find that the average coverage looks fine, yet on some days many places are missed together, and misses bunch up in time; a simple daily-scale correction helps only slightly.
summary.why: Calibrated uncertainty matters for anyone who acts on forecast ranges, and the paper suggests that a method can pass a standard average-coverage check while still failing on joint, day-level behaviour. The study is limited to one variable, one coarse grid, a reanalysis target and two forecasters, so its findings should be read as a case study rather than a general verdict.

papers.abstract: Conformal prediction gives finite-sample, distribution-free marginal coverage and has begun to be applied to gridded weather forecasts. Marginal coverage concerns the long-run fraction of covered points at a location, not how coverage behaves jointly across space and time on a given day. I benchmark eight interval-construction procedures (Gaussian, pooled and per-cell split conformal, per-season, adaptive conformal inference and rolling windows) for gridded 2 m temperature forecasts at eight lead times from 6 hours to 10 days, using ERA5 at 5.625 degree resolution, a deliberately modest convolutional forecaster and ECMWF's operational HRES, with calibration in 2017-2018 and testing in 2019-2021. Alongside coverage, width and interval score, I report dependence diagnostics: a spatial overdispersion index, quantiles of daily spatial coverage and miss persistence relative to a shuffled-days null. Per-cell methods reach near-nominal marginal coverage, yet the day-to-day variance of the fraction of cells covered is roughly 3 to 10 times what independent cells would give, and misses cluster in time; both effects grow with lead time for the CNN, also appear for HRES, and are shared by all methods. An oracle that divides each day's normalised errors by that day's mean removes 81 to 92 percent of the excess dispersion for the CNN and 93 to 98 percent for HRES, so days of large errors across much of the grid account for most of it. A day-scale predicted from seasonal terms and already-verified errors lowers the overdispersion index without widening intervals but improves interval score by at most 0.6 percent; on HRES from 12 hours to 3 days it has the lowest overdispersion index while ACI or season-conditional calibration has the best interval score, so no method is best on both. The study covers one variable, one coarse grid, a reanalysis target and two forecasters.

papers.title: What Interpolators Store and What They Express: An Information-Theoretic Framework for Benign Overfitting and Label-Free Model Selection
papers.label: arXiv:2611.23630v1

summary.background:
- Overfitting: a model fits training data too closely, including noise in the labels.
- Interpolator: a model that gets every training example exactly right.
- Benign overfitting: such a model still predicts new cases well.
- Information theory and entropy: entropy measures how much uncertainty or information a variable carries, in bits.
- Conditional mutual information (CMI): a standard information-theoretic measure of how much a model's output depends on one training example, used in generalization bounds.
- Bias-variance decomposition: splits prediction error into error from systematic assumptions and error from sensitivity to the training sample.
- Holdout validation and k-fold cross-validation: standard ways to estimate performance by reserving labelled data for testing.
- Regret (in model selection): how much worse the chosen model is than the best model in the candidate set.
summary.one_liner: The paper splits what an interpolating learner does with its training sample into storage (label information kept by the model) and expression (sample information reaching predictions at new inputs), and uses the expressed information V both to explain benign overfitting and as a label-free model-selection criterion.
summary.plain: Some machine learning models memorize noisy training labels perfectly and still predict well on new cases, which older theories struggle to explain. The paper separates what such a model stores about its training labels from what it actually passes on to its predictions, and argues that only the second part matters for how well it generalizes. The authors also propose a way to choose between models without setting aside labelled data for testing.
summary.why: It offers a new explanation for benign overfitting and a selection method that needs no held-out labels, which could matter for settings where labels are scarce. The reported gains (60% less regret than holdout validation at the same cost, comparable to 5-fold cross-validation at a quarter of the cost, on 15 noisy datasets) come from the authors' experiments; I have not verified them, and the approach is limited to cases where the authors say it fails under certain conditions.

papers.abstract: Overparameterized learners can fit noisy training labels perfectly and still predict well, which neither classical complexity measures nor information-theoretic generalization bounds explain. We develop an information-theoretic framework that separates two things an interpolating learner does with its sample: storage, the information the trained model retains about its training labels, and expression, the information about the sample that reaches its predictions at fresh inputs. We first characterize the ideal model: for a loss l, the least complex l-sufficient representation is the Bayes act, whose entropy is the minimal sufficient complexity; this generalizes, and corrects, an earlier "lossless maximal compression" view of boosting. We then show that every interpolator stores exactly nH(Y|X) bits of label noise, so storage, and bounds built on it (including CMI bounds), cannot tell interpolators apart. Expression can: excess risk is bounded above and below by the expressed information V, the entropy over training samples of the prediction at an input, plus a modal-bias term, exactly so for binary labels. Benign overfitting is therefore vanishing expression, a picture that covers nearest-neighbour rules, averaging, minimum-norm least squares and double descent, and that links V to classical bias-variance decompositions and to model disagreement. Finally, V gives a model-selection criterion that needs no held-out labels. Among overparameterized learners on 15 noisy datasets, V estimated from two disjoint halves has 60% less regret than holdout validation at the same cost and matches 5-fold cross-validation at a quarter of its cost; at matched cost it also beats selection by conditional mutual information. We characterize when it fails and give remedies. Code: https://github.com/nnikolaou/GLMC

papers.title: The Price of Hard Coverage Constraints in Online Conformal Prediction
papers.label: arXiv:2611.22646v1

summary.background:
- Prediction set: instead of one guess, a method outputs a set of plausible outcomes; bigger sets are more likely to contain the truth but are less informative.
- Miscoverage: an event where the true outcome falls outside the predicted set.
- Coverage guarantee: a promise about how often the true outcome lands inside the set, typically on average.
- Online setting: predictions are made one round at a time, with data arriving sequentially.
- Hard (cumulative) budget: the total number of misses must stay under a limit at all times, not just on average.
- Big-O / Theta notation: Theta(f(T)) means the cost grows at the same rate as f(T) up to constant factors.
- Regularity conditions: mathematical assumptions the authors need for the exact rates to hold; the text says these are required but does not list them.
summary.one_liner: The paper characterizes the unavoidable extra prediction-set size needed by online conformal prediction methods that must keep cumulative miscoverages within a hard budget over T rounds, showing the cost holds even with i.i.d. data and known score distribution.
summary.plain: The paper looks at a forecasting-with-safety-margin problem: a system makes a set of possible answers each round and must keep the number of times the true answer is missed under a fixed budget over the whole run. The authors show that enforcing this strict budget forces the sets to grow by a minimum amount, and they pin down how that minimum scales with the number of rounds. The extra cost depends on which kind of time horizon is being judged, growing like log T, T^(1/3), or the square root of T in different cases.
summary.why: Conformal prediction is widely used to attach reliability guarantees to predictions, so knowing the exact price of a strict, cumulative guarantee is useful for deployment decisions. The result is theoretical, and the text does not say how it would translate to specific practical systems.

papers.abstract: Conformal prediction provides distribution-free uncertainty quantification, but in sequential deployment, standard coverage guarantees can still allow substantial fluctuations in the number of miscoverages over time. We study an online setting in which prediction sets are produced one round at a time and the cumulative number of miscoverages must stay within a prescribed budget throughout deployment.Such a hard coverage guarantee can be enforced by enlarging prediction sets, but how much additional prediction-set size is fundamentally necessary remains unclear. We characterize this unavoidable efficiency cost over $T$ prediction rounds. Remarkably, the cost persists even with i.i.d.\ data, a known score distribution, and perfect knowledge of the population-optimal prediction set. Under suitable regularity conditions relating coverage and prediction-set size, we determine the minimum cumulative excess prediction-set size required by any online method satisfying the hard coverage constraint. This minimum cost is $Θ(\log T)$ for expected cost at a fixed time known in advance, $Θ(T^{1/3})$ for the largest expected cost over all fixed times up to $T$, and $Θ(\sqrt{T})$ for the expected worst realized cost when the evaluation time is chosen in hindsight. We further show that these rates can be attained using past scores, without knowing the score distribution. Thus, even perfect statistical knowledge does not make sequential reliability free.

papers.title: Bellman Residual Bracketing: Resolving the Sample Complexity of Discounted and Average-Reward RL
papers.label: arXiv:2611.19566v1

summary.background:
- Reinforcement learning (RL): an agent learns by acting in an environment and receiving rewards.
- Generative model: a simulator the agent can query for any state and action to get a next state and reward.
- Sample complexity: how many queries or data points are needed to reach a target accuracy.
- Discount factor (gamma): how strongly future rewards are weighted against immediate ones; the effective horizon grows like 1/(1-gamma).
- Average-reward setting: the goal is long-run reward per step, with no discounting.
- Plug-in approach: estimate the transition and reward model from data, then solve that estimated model exactly.
- Bellman residual: how much a value estimate violates the Bellman optimality equation.
- Minimax rate: the best worst-case guarantee achievable by any method, matched by an upper and lower bound.
- Span and diameter: measures of how spread out values or reachable states are in an average-reward problem.
summary.one_liner: The paper proves sample-complexity bounds for plug-in (empirical model-based) planning in discounted and average-reward reinforcement learning with a generative model, using a new Bellman residual bracketing technique, and claims these match lower bounds up to constant factors.
summary.plain: The paper studies how much experience a learning agent needs to find a nearly best strategy in a decision-making problem, assuming it can query a simulator for any state-action pair. The approach is "plug-in" planning: estimate the problem's rules from sampled data, then solve the estimated problem. The authors state upper bounds on how many samples this needs and say that, paired with earlier lower bounds, these settle the minimax sample complexity in the settings they cover.
summary.why: Sample complexity questions ask how much data is fundamentally required, so pinning down the exact rate is a useful theoretical milestone if the claims hold. The new analysis technique (bracketing the Bellman residual, a measure of how far a value estimate is from satisfying the optimality equation) is presented as a way to make earlier absorbing-MDP-based proofs more efficient. Whether this changes practice is unclear from the abstract alone.

papers.abstract: We study the sample complexity of the empirical planning or plug-in approach for reinforcement learning (RL) with a generative model. We show the discounted plug-in approach finds an $\varepsilon$-optimal policy with $O(SA (1-γ)^{-3} \varepsilon^{-2} \log(SA/δ))$ samples, where $S, A, γ, δ$ are the state and action sizes, discount factor, and failure probability, respectively. In the average-reward setting, we show that discounted plug-in and direct (undiscounted) plug-in achieve $O(SAH\varepsilon^{-2}\log(SA/δ))$ and $O(SAD\varepsilon^{-2}\log(SA/δ))$ complexities, respectively, where $H$ upper-bounds the optimal bias span and $D$ is the diameter. Combining with our lower bounds for nonadaptive generative models, these results resolve the minimax sample complexity of discounted RL and average-reward RL --- in both the span- and diameter-based classes --- up to constant factors. Our main technical contribution is a novel Bellman residual bracketing technique which improves the efficiency of prior absorbing-MDP-based concentration analyses.

papers.title: The cost of enforcing long-run coverage: a phase transition in online conformal prediction
papers.label: arXiv:2611.21542v1

summary.background:
- Prediction interval / prediction set: a range (or set of labels) that should contain the true outcome with a chosen probability, here 1 minus alpha.
- Coverage: the fraction of times the true outcome actually falls inside the range.
- Exchangeable / i.i.d. data: the order of observations does not matter statistically; i.i.d. means each is an independent draw from the same distribution.
- Split conformal prediction: a standard method that builds valid prediction ranges from a held-out set of past residuals or scores.
- Online and adversarial settings: data arrive one at a time and may be chosen by an opponent or shift over time, so no distributional assumption is made.
- Long-run versus instantaneous coverage: average coverage over many steps versus coverage at each individual step conditional on the training data.
- Phase transition: a sharp change in behavior when a parameter crosses a threshold; here, at beta = 1/2.
- Big-O notation: O(T^-beta) means the deviation shrinks at roughly the rate T to the power minus beta as the horizon T grows.
summary.one_liner: The paper characterizes, via a phase transition at exponent β = 1/2, when online conformal prediction can keep long-run coverage within O(T^-β) of the target in adversarial settings while matching split conformal prediction's per-step coverage in the i.i.d. case.
summary.plain: The paper looks at a forecasting task where a model must give a range of likely outcomes for each new data point, one after another. The usual guarantee for such ranges holds when data behave like repeated fair draws, but real streams can drift or change abruptly. The authors study how tightly one can control the average coverage over time without making the ranges jump around when the data are in fact well behaved.
summary.why: The result is a sharp threshold: tight long-run control is achievable at no cost up to a certain strictness, and beyond it a trade-off appears. This is a theoretical statement, and the text does not show practical experiments, so its impact on deployed systems is unclear from this text alone.

papers.abstract: Consider an online prediction setting, where at each time, we are given a new feature vector and asked to provide a prediction interval or prediction set that will likely contain the corresponding response. In this setting, if the data points are i.i.d. (or more generally, exchangeable), conformal prediction provides a mechanism for building valid prediction sets around the output of any trained model, offering coverage probability $\geq 1-α$ at each time $t$. In practice, however, issues such as distribution drift, changepoints, or other challenges may cause violations of the i.i.d. assumption. In this adversarial setting, online conformal prediction methods can still offer guarantees on long-run empirical coverage. However, there is a trade-off between these two types of goals: enforcing tight constraints on long-run empirical coverage to protect against the adversarial setting can lead to unstable oscillations in the instantaneous training-conditional coverage in the i.i.d. setting. In this work, we seek best-of-both-worlds algorithms that aim to minimize cumulative error in instantaneous training-conditional coverage when in the i.i.d. setting, while also offering long-run empirical coverage guarantees in the adversarial setting. Specifically, consider a condition that requires long-run empirical coverage to deviate from the target level $1-α$ by at most $\mathcal{O}(T^{-β})$, for some $β\in[0,1]$. We prove that this family of conditions can be described with a phase transition. For $β\in[0,\frac{1}{2}]$, it is possible to construct algorithms satisfying such a constraint in the adversarial setting, while offering the same instantaneous coverage performance as split conformal prediction if the data is in fact i.i.d. On the other hand, for $β\in(\frac{1}{2},1]$, this type of condition comes at a cost, and does not achieve best-of-both-worlds behavior.
